transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I get stuck in front of the mirror or looking at photos of myself, trying to fix how I look, and it’s starting to mess with my work and my runs. It's just taking up so much of my time lately, and I realized I need to get some help for it.

When you spend this time looking in the mirror, are you primarily focused on a specific perceived flaw in your appearance that you are trying to hide or fix, or are you performing these behaviors to reduce distress caused by repetitive, intrusive thoughts?

Yes, I'm completely focused on specific flaws on my face, like how my nose looks bent, my jaw looks totally off, and my skin looks like old leather. I get stuck in front of the mirror tilting my head to check if I look lopsided, trying to "fix" it because I'm so anxious about how other people see me. It really is about trying to correct those specific parts of my face.
Do you feel that these specific features of your face are genuinely deformed or ugly to others, or do you recognize that your perception might be exaggerated or distorted?

To me, these flaws feel completely real and obvious, not like I'm just exaggerating. I genuinely see my face as battered and crooked, with a bent nose and an off-jaw, and I constantly worry about how anyone can even stand to look at me. Even when I ask my family for reassurance, the deformity feels 100% real in my mind.

The behaviors (mirror checking, tilting head) are performed to address these perceived defects, and the preoccupation causes significant functional impairment in work and personal activities.
